topic_tag: law of cosines applied twice in a quadrilateral
subskill: diagonal by law of cosines, then a side by law of cosines
prompt: In quadrilateral ABCD, AB = 7 meters, BC = 12 meters, the measure of angle ABC is 75°, CD = 9 meters, and the measure of angle ACD is 52°. Points B and D lie on opposite sides of diagonal AC. To the nearest hundredth of a meter, what is the length of AD ? (Note: For any triangle with sides a, b, and c, where C is the angle opposite side c, c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C.)
explanation: In triangle ABC, AC² = 7² + 12² − 2(7)(12)cos 75° ≈ 193 − 43.48 = 149.52, so AC ≈ 12.228. In triangle ACD, the angle at C between AC and CD is 52°, so AD² = AC² + 9² − 2(AC)(9)cos 52° ≈ 149.52 + 81 − 135.51 = 95.01, and AD ≈ 9.75. The option "9.59" rounds AC to 12 before the second step. The option "7.55" uses sin 52° in place of cos 52° in the second step. The option "7.09" uses sin 75° in place of cos 75° in the first step.
quantity_asked: the length AD, found from AC ≈ 12.228 (law of cosines in ABC) and then AD² = AC² + 81 − 18·AC·cos 52°: AD ≈ 9.75 m.

distractor_kind.9.59: intermediate rounding: AC rounded to 12 before the second step. (a) no parameter extreme. (b) neighbouring setup: AD as a function of AC is increasing here, but AC = 12 is not a stem-forced bound. (c) cheapest bounds: angle ABC < 90° gives AC < √(7² + 12²) ≈ 13.89 and AC > 12 − 7 = 5; converting either into a bound on AD needs the second law-of-cosines step (the work); the only stem-direct bounds on AD are 0 < AD < AB + BC + CD = 28 and AD < AC + CD; 9.46 strictly inside. (d) real: premature rounding.
distractor_kind.7.55: sine for cosine in the second step. (a) no. (b) none. (c) inside. (d) real: sin/cos confusion in c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C.
distractor_kind.7.09: sine for cosine in the first step (AC ≈ 5.54), then the second step done correctly. (a) no. (b) none. (c) inside (AD > AC − CD needs AC). (d) real: sin/cos confusion at the other step.

arith_class_check: Two-decimal irrational lengths; no integrality or divisibility is implied; the key is not lone in any class.
one_sided_check: Key largest. Three errors at three different steps (rounding, step-2 trig, step-1 trig). Not stem-readable: rounding lowers AD only because 12.228 rounds down, and each sin-for-cos slip shortens the side only because both given angles exceed 45° (sin > cos); with an angle under 45° the same slip lengthens it. The student cannot see these directions without doing the computation.
interior_parity_check: Interior options by value: 7.55 and 9.59 - both two-decimal with nonzero final digit; equally clean.
cheap_bound_check: Cheapest one-sided bounds on AD read off the stem are AD < 28 (path through B and C) and, after AC, AD > AC − 9 ≈ 3.23 and AD < AC + 9; all three distractors lie on the key's side of each. Nearest distractor 9.59 is 1.6% below the key (a rounding-stage error), inside the resolution of any estimate short of the full computation.

self_audit.note: Largest key; nearest distractor is a rounding-stage slip 2% away; no stem bound separates; live rows use one law-of-cosines step, not a two-triangle chain.

topic_tag: perpendicular chords and the radius of a circle
subskill: radius from two perpendicular intersecting chords
prompt: Chords AB and CD of a circle are perpendicular and intersect at point P inside the circle. AP = 5 inches, PB = 8 inches, and CP = 4 inches. To the nearest hundredth of an inch, what is the radius of the circle?
explanation: By the intersecting-chords relationship, AP·PB = CP·PD, so PD = 40/4 = 10 and CD = 14, AB = 13. The center O is on the perpendicular bisector of each chord. The midpoint of CD is 7 − 4 = 3 inches from P along CD, and that offset is the distance from O to line AB (the chords are perpendicular). So O is 3 inches from AB, and AB has half-length 6.5: r = √(6.5² + 3²) = √51.25 ≈ 7.16. (Check with CD: the midpoint of AB is 1.5 from P, so r = √(7² + 1.5²) ≈ 7.16.) The option "7.62" pairs the half-length of CD with the distance to AB, √(7² + 3²). The option "7.76" uses the power of P, r² = AP·PB + OP², but takes OP as 3 + 1.5 instead of √(3² + 1.5²). The option "8.85" forgets to halve the offset, using √(6.5² + 6²).
quantity_asked: the radius of the circle, √(6.5² + 3²) ≈ 7.16, after PD = 10 from AP·PB = CP·PD.

distractor_kind.7.62: mismatched pairing: half of CD with the distance from O to AB. (a) no parameter extreme. (b) neighbouring setup: neither chord's own right triangle; not a bound. (c) cheapest bounds: r ≥ CD/2 = 7 (chord ≤ diameter) and r > PD/2 = 5; no cheap upper bound; 7.62 strictly inside. (d) real: pairs the wrong half-chord with the wrong offset.
distractor_kind.7.76: power of a point with OP added instead of combined by the Pythagorean theorem. (a) no. (b) none. (c) inside [7, ∞). (d) real: r² = PA·PB + OP² is right; OP = 3 + 1.5 is the slip.
distractor_kind.8.85: offset not halved: the distance from O to AB taken as PD − CP = 6 instead of (PD − CP)/2. (a) no. (b) none. (c) inside [7, 9.55): the distance from O to AB is less than CD/2 = 7, so r < √(6.5² + 7²) ≈ 9.55. (d) real: forgets that the chord midpoint is halfway.

bounds: v ≥ CD/2 = 7 (a chord is at most a diameter)
v < √(6.5² + 7²) ≈ 9.55 (distance from O to AB < CD/2)
mechanism: radius from half-chord and distance to center
arith_class_check: Two-decimal irrational lengths throughout; no integrality or divisibility is implied, and the key (√51.25) is not lone in any class.
one_sided_check: Key smallest. Three different error kinds (wrong pairing, OP by addition, offset not halved). The stem gives no way to tell which way a mis-paired triangle moves r without computing both offsets; the pairing error lands below the key whenever the shorter chord is the one paired (e.g. half of AB with the distance to CD gives 6.67 here), so the direction is not readable from the stem.
interior_parity_check: Interior options by value: 7.62 and 7.76 - both two-decimal with nonzero final digit; equally clean.
cheap_bound_check: Cheapest bounds: r ≥ CD/2 = 7 (chord ≤ diameter), which lies BELOW the key 7.16, and r < √(6.5² + 7²) ≈ 9.55, above every option. There is no cheap upper bound between 7.16 and 7.62; the nearest distractor is 6.4% above the key and separating them needs both offsets, i.e. the work.

self_audit.note: Smallest key; the only cheap bound (r ≥ 7) sits below it; three distinct errors. Chord-distance sub-step exists live (sat 4ad0761e) but not the perpendicular-chords setup.

topic_tag: region between two tangent circles and a common tangent line
prompt: Two circles, with radii of 9 inches and 6 inches, are tangent to each other, and both circles are tangent to the same straight line on the same side of it. A small region is enclosed by the line and the two circles. To the nearest hundredth of a square inch, what is the area of that region?
explanation: Let the circles touch the line at T₁ and T₂, with centers O₁ (radius 9) and O₂ (radius 6). The centers are 9 + 6 = 15 apart and their heights differ by 3, so T₁T₂ = √(15² − 3²) = √216 ≈ 14.70. Trapezoid O₁T₁T₂O₂ has area (1/2)(9 + 6)(14.70) ≈ 110.23. The angle at O₁ between O₁T₁ and O₁O₂ has cosine 3/15, so it measures about 78.46°, and the angle at O₂ is 180° − 78.46° = 101.54°. Subtracting the two sectors, (78.46/360)π(9²) ≈ 55.46 and (101.54/360)π(6²) ≈ 31.90, leaves about 22.87. The option "18.34" treats each sector as a quarter circle. The option "25.14" takes the distance between the points of tangency to be the distance between the centers, 15. The option "30.11" uses the 78.46° angle for both sectors.
quantity_asked: the area enclosed by the common tangent line and the two tangent circles (radii 9 and 6): trapezoid (1/2)(15)√216 minus sectors of 78.46° (radius 9) and 101.54° (radius 6) ≈ 22.87 in².

distractor_kind.18.34: both sectors taken as quarter circles (90° each). (a) no parameter extreme. (b) neighbouring setup: the right-angle case is not stem-forced and not a bound - the two angles sum to 180° whatever the radii. (c) cheapest bounds: area > 0; the region lies inside triangle T₁T₂K (K the point where the circles touch, height 9 − 3·9/15 = 7.2), area ≈ (1/2)(14.70)(7.2) ≈ 52.91, which already needs T₁T₂; 18.34 strictly inside. (d) real: assumes the radii to the tangency points meet the center line at right angles.
distractor_kind.25.14: center distance used as the tangent-point distance. (a) no. (b) none. (c) inside (0, 52.91). (d) real: T₁T₂ confused with O₁O₂.
distractor_kind.30.11: one angle used for both sectors. (a) no. (b) none. (c) inside (0, 52.91). (d) real: forgets that the two angles are supplementary.

mechanism: two mutually tangent circles on a line
curvilinear region between circles and tangent line
arith_class_check: Two-decimal areas from π and a square root; nothing implies integrality or divisibility; the key is not lone in any class.
interior_parity_check: Interior options by value: 22.87 and 25.14 - both two-decimal with nonzero final digit; equally clean.

self_audit.note: Interior key, all inside (0, 52.91). The T₁T₂ step matches live act 4197bc84 (tangent-point distance); the asked area, trapezoid minus sectors, has no live row.

topic_tag: area of a region between two arcs (annular sector)
subskill: area swept by a blade offset from the pivot
prompt: A windshield wiper arm is 50 centimeters long from its pivot to its tip. The rubber blade is attached along the outer 35 centimeters of the arm, so the blade runs from 15 centimeters to 50 centimeters from the pivot. The arm rotates back and forth through an angle of 118°. To the nearest square centimeter, what is the area of the region of the windshield that the blade wipes?
explanation: The wiped region is the part of a 118° sector of radius 50 that lies outside the 118° sector of radius 15. With θ = 118π/180 ≈ 2.0595 radians, the area is (1/2)θ(50² − 15²) = (1/2)(2.0595)(2,275) ≈ 2,343. The option "2475" subtracts the triangle with two 15-cm sides and a 118° angle, (1/2)(15²) sin 118°, instead of the small sector. The option "2559" subtracts 15 instead of 15². The option "1313" takes 35 as the inner radius, (1/2)θ(50² − 35²).
quantity_asked: the area between the 118° arcs of radii 15 and 50, (1/2)(118π/180)(50² − 15²) ≈ 2,343 cm².

distractor_kind.1313: blade length taken as the inner radius. (a) no. (b) none. (c) inside (0, 2,574). (d) real: confuses which radius the 35 is.
distractor_kind.2475: inner triangle subtracted instead of the inner sector. (a) no parameter extreme. (b) neighbouring setup: outer sector minus inner triangle is not a bound on the region. (c) cheapest bounds: area < the 118° sector of radius 50 ≈ 2,574 and area > 0; 2475 strictly inside. (d) real: sector/triangle confusion.
distractor_kind.2559: inner radius not squared. (a) no. (b) none. (c) inside: 2,559 < 2,574 strictly. (d) real: r² slip.

arith_class_check: Whole-number areas rounded from π-multiples; no divisibility or parity property is implied; the key is not lone in any class.
interior_parity_check: Interior options by value: 2343 and 2475 - both four-digit whole numbers ending in a nonzero digit; equally clean.

self_audit.note: Interior key; every option strictly under the outer-sector cap 2,574; no live wiper/annular-sector row.

topic_tag: triangle inscribed in a circle from its arcs
subskill: inscribed triangle area from central angles
prompt: Points P, Q, and R lie on a circle with a radius of 8 meters. The three minor arcs PQ, QR, and RP measure 80°, 130°, and 150°, respectively. To the nearest hundredth of a square meter, what is the area of triangle PQR ?
explanation: Join each vertex to the center O. Because every arc is less than 180°, O is inside the triangle, which splits into three isosceles triangles with two sides of 8 and apex angles 80°, 130°, and 150°. The area is (1/2)(8²)(sin 80° + sin 130° + sin 150°) = 32(0.9848 + 0.7660 + 0.5) ≈ 72.03. The option "80.48" uses half of each arc (40°, 65°, 75°) in this central-angle formula. The option "67.58" finds PQ = 16 sin 40° and QR = 16 sin 65° but uses 65° instead of the 75° inscribed angle at Q between them. The option "51.08" finds PQ = 16 sin 40° and PR = 16 sin 75° but uses 40° instead of the 65° inscribed angle at P between them.
quantity_asked: the area of the triangle whose vertices cut the circle of radius 8 into arcs of 80°, 130°, 150°: 32(sin 80° + sin 130° + sin 150°) ≈ 72.03 m².

distractor_kind.80.48: inscribed angles used where central angles belong. (a) no parameter extreme. (b) neighbouring setup: not the area of any inscribed triangle here; not a bound. (c) cheapest bounds: each central triangle has area at least (1/2)(64) sin 150° = 16, so area ≥ 48; area ≤ the equilateral maximum (3√3/4)(64) ≈ 83.14; 80.48 strictly inside. (d) real: halves the arcs at the wrong step.
distractor_kind.67.58: wrong inscribed angle between the two chords. (a) no. (b) none. (c) inside (48, 83.14). (d) real: picks the inscribed angle at R instead of at Q.
distractor_kind.51.08: wrong inscribed angle at P (the one subtending PQ). (a) no. (b) none. (c) inside (48, 83.14). (d) real: uses the angle opposite the wrong chord.

mechanism: area = (1/2)r² sin θ for each central triangle
inscribed angle is half the arc
arith_class_check: Two-decimal areas from sines; no integrality or divisibility is implied; the key is not lone in any class.
interior_parity_check: Interior options by value: 67.58 and 72.03 - both two-decimal with nonzero final digit; equally clean.

self_audit.note: Interior key; all options inside (48, 83.14); live arc rows ask an inscribed angle (act 51a57e01), not an area.

topic_tag: inscribed and circumscribed circles of a right triangle
prompt: In the standard (x,y) coordinate plane, a right triangle has vertices (0, 0), (10, 0), and (0, 6). To the nearest hundredth of a coordinate unit, what is the distance between the center of the circle inscribed in the triangle and the center of the circle circumscribed about the triangle?
explanation: The hypotenuse is √(10² + 6²) = √136 ≈ 11.662. The circumcenter of a right triangle is the midpoint of the hypotenuse, (5, 3). The inscribed circle is tangent to both legs, so its center is (r, r), where r = (area)/(semiperimeter) = 30/13.831 = (10 + 6 − √136)/2 ≈ 2.169. The distance is √((5 − 2.169)² + (3 − 2.169)²) ≈ 2.95. The option "4.36" uses r = area/perimeter ≈ 1.085. The option "3.07" takes the circumcenter at the right-angle vertex (0, 0), the orthocenter, giving r√2. The option "3.66" assumes the distance is R − r = 5.831 − 2.169.
quantity_asked: the distance from the incenter (r, r), r = (16 − √136)/2, to the circumcenter (5, 3) of the right triangle (0,0), (10,0), (0,6): ≈ 2.95.

distractor_kind.4.36: inradius as area/perimeter. (a) no parameter extreme. (b) neighbouring setup: (r, r) with r = 1.085 is not a stem-forced bound. (c) cheapest bounds: both centers are inside the triangle and the circumcenter is on the hypotenuse, so the distance is less than the circumradius 5.83; 4.36 strictly inside. (d) real: r = A/s confused with A/P.
distractor_kind.3.07: circumcenter confused with the orthocenter (the right-angle vertex). (a) no. (b) none. (c) inside (0, 5.83). (d) real: in a right triangle the orthocenter is the right-angle vertex.
distractor_kind.3.66: distance taken as R − r (as if the incircle were internally tangent to the circumcircle along a line through both centers). (a) no. (b) none. (c) inside. (d) real: a formula guess from the two radii.

mechanism: circumcenter of a right triangle is the hypotenuse midpoint
arith_class_check: Two-decimal irrational distances; no integrality or divisibility is implied, and the key is not lone in any class.
one_sided_check: Key smallest. Three different error kinds (A/P inradius, orthocenter for circumcenter, R − r). Their directions are not stem-readable: taking the centroid as the circumcenter (another natural slip) gives 1.18 and doubling r gives 1.49, both below the key, so a student cannot infer that wrong methods overshoot.
interior_parity_check: Interior options by value: 3.07 and 3.66 - both two-decimal with nonzero final digit; equally clean.
cheap_bound_check: Cheapest one-sided bound: distance < circumradius 5.83 (upper; above every option). One step finer, bracketing √136 between 11 and 12 gives r = (16 − √136)/2 in (2, 3) and the distance in (2, 3.16): that removes 3.66 and 4.36 but leaves 3.07 on the key's side; it uses the inradius formula, which is the core of the work. No bound falls between the key 2.95 and the nearest distractor 3.07 (4% above).

self_audit.note: Bracketing √136 in (11, 12) puts r in (2, 3) and the distance in (2, 3.16), removing 3.66 and 4.36; it needs the inradius step, but a grader may count it.

topic_tag: dividing a triangle into equal areas with a vertical line
subskill: area of a similar sub-triangle cut by a vertical line
prompt: In the standard (x,y) coordinate plane, a triangle has vertices (0, 0), (11, 0), and (3, 6). The vertical line x = c divides the triangle into two regions of equal area. To the nearest hundredth, what is the value of c ?
explanation: The triangle's area is (1/2)(11)(6) = 33, so each region has area 16.5. The part of the triangle to the left of x = 3 has area (1/2)(3)(6) = 9 < 16.5, so c > 3. To the right of x = c, the region is a triangle with vertices (c, 0), (11, 0), and (c, (6/8)(11 − c)), with area (3/8)(11 − c)². Setting (3/8)(11 − c)² = 16.5 gives (11 − c)² = 44 and c = 11 − √44 ≈ 4.37. The option "4.06" uses the formula for the left region as if it were still a triangle with apex height 2c, (1/2)(c)(2c) = 16.5. The option "3.85" is the x-coordinate of the center of the inscribed circle. The option "3.22" treats the right region as similar to the whole triangle, 11 − 11/√2.
quantity_asked: the x-value c at which the vertical line splits the triangle (0,0), (11,0), (3,6) into two regions of area 16.5: c = 11 − √44 ≈ 4.37.

distractor_kind.4.06: left-piece formula used past the apex: (1/2)c(2c) = 16.5. (a) no parameter extreme. (b) neighbouring setup: the formula is right only for c ≤ 3; its value is not a bound. (c) cheapest bounds: 3 < c (left part at x = 3 has area 9) and c < 5.5 (the median from (3, 6) meets the base at 5.5, and the region left of x = 5.5 contains more than half); one step finer, at c = 4 the right triangle has area (3/8)(49) = 18.4 > 16.5, so c > 4: 4.06 is strictly above 4, inside. (d) real: keeps using the wrong piece of a piecewise area.
distractor_kind.3.85: line through the incenter assumed to bisect the area. (a) no. (b) none. (c) inside (3, 5.5) but below the finer bound c > 4 - see cheap_bound_check. (d) real: misremembers "lines through the incenter that bisect the perimeter also bisect the area".
distractor_kind.3.22: right region treated as similar to the whole triangle. (a) no. (b) none. (c) inside (3, 5.5). (d) real: wrong similar triangle.

bounds: v > 4 (right triangle at c = 4 has area 18.4 > 16.5)
mechanism: vertical line bisecting a triangle's area
piecewise area of a triangle cut by x = c
arith_class_check: Two-decimal irrational values; no integrality or divisibility is implied, and the key (11 − √44) is not lone in any class.
one_sided_check: Key largest. Three different error kinds (wrong piece, incenter line, wrong similar triangle). Not stem-readable: the most common slip, the centroid line x = 14/3 ≈ 4.67, lands ABOVE the key, as does scaling the right sub-triangle (5.34).
interior_parity_check: Interior options by value: 3.85 and 4.06 - both two-decimal with nonzero final digit; equally clean.
cheap_bound_check: Cheapest bounds: c > 3 (left part at the apex holds only 9) and c < 5.5 (median foot). One step finer: at c = 4 the right part is (3/8)(7²) = 18.375 > 16.5, so c > 4 - this kills 3.22 and 3.85 but the nearest distractor 4.06 lies on the KEY's side of it. Separating 4.06 from 4.37 needs the work.

self_audit.note: Largest key; the c > 4 check removes two distractors (survivors 2 by a one-step test) - 4.06 survives it, but a grader may still call the item thin.

topic_tag: exponential growth and decay acting together
subskill: combining two exponential factors with different periods
prompt: A culture of 1,840 bacteria grows exponentially and, with nothing else acting on it, would double every 3 hours. An antibiotic is added at the start; acting alone, it would reduce the number of bacteria exponentially by 22% every 4 hours. The two effects act together, so their growth and decay factors multiply. To the nearest whole number, how many bacteria are there 7 hours after the start?
explanation: The number after t hours is N(t) = 1,840 · 2^(t/3) · 0.78^(t/4), so N(7) = 1,840 · 2^(7/3) · 0.78^(7/4) ≈ 1,840 · 5.0397 · 0.64759 ≈ 6,003. The option "5741" counts only completed periods for both effects (2 doublings and 1 reduction): 1,840 · 4 · 0.78. The option "5193" uses the 3-hour period in the decay exponent, 0.78^(7/3). The option "4765" counts only the 2 completed doublings but applies the decay continuously, 1,840 · 4 · 0.78^(7/4).

distractor_kind.4765: whole doublings only, continuous decay. (a) no. (b) none. (c) inside (4,478, 11,482). (d) real: floors the growth exponent.
distractor_kind.5193: decay exponent uses the growth period (t/3 for both). (a) no. (b) none. (c) inside (4,478, 11,482). (d) real: one period applied to both factors.
distractor_kind.5741: whole periods only, for both effects. (a) no parameter extreme. (b) neighbouring setup: the step-function model; not a bound (truncating the doubling lowers N, truncating the decay raises it). (c) cheapest bounds: 2^(7/3) is between 2² and 2³ and 0.78^(7/4) between 0.78² and 0.78, so 1,840·4·0.6084 ≈ 4,478 < N < 1,840·8·0.78 ≈ 11,482; 5741 strictly inside. (d) real: treats continuous change as discrete events.

mechanism: doubling time and percent decay per period
arith_class_check: Whole-number counts; the key and all distractors are four-digit integers with no common factor pattern; no divisibility or parity property is implied, and the key is not lone in any class.
one_sided_check: Key largest. Two error families (period counting; wrong period in an exponent). Not stem-readable: flooring the DECAY exponent alone raises N (to 7,233 here), and dividing the 22% across hours raises it too, so a student cannot infer that slips undershoot.
interior_parity_check: Interior options by value: 5193 and 5741 - both four-digit integers ending in a nonzero digit; equally clean.
cheap_bound_check: Cheapest bound: bracketing each exponent between neighbouring integers gives 4,478 < N < 11,482; all three distractors lie on the key's side (inside). One step finer needs 2^(1/3) and 0.78^(3/4), which is the work. Nearest distractor 5741 is 4.4% below the key.

self_audit.note: Largest key; integer-bracket bound leaves all three inside; two floor variants are distinct steps with opposite single effects.

topic_tag: sum of two exponential decay functions
subskill: total of two decaying quantities with different half-lives
prompt: A sample contains 30 grams of substance A, which has a half-life of 4 hours, and 120 grams of substance B, which has a half-life of 16 hours. Each substance decays exponentially and independently of the other. To the nearest hundredth of a gram, what is the total mass of A and B remaining 9 hours later?
explanation: A(t) = 30(1/2)^(t/4) and B(t) = 120(1/2)^(t/16). At t = 9: A = 30(0.5)^2.25 ≈ 6.31 and B = 120(0.5)^0.5625 ≈ 81.25, for a total of about 87.56 grams. The option "86.25" assumes each substance loses mass at a constant rate of half its starting mass per half-life, so A is gone after 8 hours and B = 120(1 − 9/32). The option "80.38" applies the average half-life, 10 hours, to all 150 grams. The option "71.54" uses e^(−t/T) as if each half-life were a time constant.

distractor_kind.86.25: linear decay at half the initial mass per half-life (A exhausted at 8 h). (a) no parameter extreme. (b) neighbouring setup: the linear model is not a bound on the total (above the exponential for B, below for A). (c) cheapest bounds, bracketing each exponent between half-integers: 2.25 ∈ (2, 2.5) gives A ∈ (5.30, 7.5); 0.5625 ∈ (0.5, 1) gives B ∈ (60, 84.85); total ∈ (65.30, 92.35); 86.25 strictly inside. (d) real: linear-decay misconception.
distractor_kind.80.38: average half-life applied to the total. (a) no. (b) none. (c) inside (65.30, 92.35). (d) real: merges the substances.
distractor_kind.71.54: e as the base with the half-life as time constant. (a) no. (b) none. (c) inside (65.30, 92.35). (d) real: confuses half-life with e-folding time.

arith_class_check: Two-decimal masses; no integrality or divisibility property is implied; the key is not lone in any class.
one_sided_check: Key largest. Three different error kinds. Not stem-readable: the linear model overshoots for the long-half-life substance and undershoots for the short one, and the average half-life overshoots whenever the larger mass has the shorter half-life; only these numbers put all three below.
interior_parity_check: Interior options by value: 80.38 and 86.25 - both two-decimal with nonzero final digit; equally clean.
cheap_bound_check: Cheapest bound: bracket each exponent between half-integers (using 2^(−1/2) ≈ 0.707): total ∈ (65.30, 92.35); all three distractors are on the key's side (inside). Nearest distractor 86.25 is 1.5% below the key; separating them needs 0.5^0.5625, i.e. the work.

self_audit.note: Largest key; half-step exponent brackets leave all three inside; live act 878fea56 equates two colonies (a different ask).

topic_tag: rational function model with a parameter
subskill: fit a rational model from one point, then solve
prompt: A typing student's speed, in words per minute, after t weeks of practice is modeled by the function W(t) = 70t/(t + k), where k is a positive constant. After 3 weeks of practice, the student types 40 words per minute. According to the model, after how many weeks of practice, to the nearest hundredth, will the student type 59 words per minute?
explanation: From W(3) = 40: 210/(3 + k) = 40, so 3 + k = 5.25 and k = 2.25. Then 70t/(t + 2.25) = 59 gives 70t = 59t + 132.75, so 11t = 132.75 and t ≈ 12.07. The option "14.32" makes a slip in the last step, 70t = 59t + 70(2.25), so t = 157.5/11. The option "21.45" finds k from the reciprocal ratio, k = 3·40/30 = 4. The option "28.16" forgets to subtract 3 when solving for k, using k = 210/40 = 5.25.

distractor_kind.14.32: final-step slip: 70·k instead of 59·k on the right. (a) no parameter extreme. (b) neighbouring setup: none. (c) cheapest bounds: W is increasing and W(3) = 40 < 59, so t > 3; W approaches 70, so no finite upper bound is cheap; 14.32 strictly inside. (d) real: wrong constant carried across.
distractor_kind.21.45: k from the inverted ratio, k = 3·40/30. (a) no. (b) none. (c) inside (3, ∞). (d) real: solves 40 = 70·3/(3 + k) upside down.
distractor_kind.28.16: k = 210/40 without subtracting 3. (a) no. (b) none. (c) inside. (d) real: forgets the t in t + k.

28.16.error_kind: forgot to subtract t0 for k

mechanism: solve for parameter from one data point
arith_class_check: Two-decimal values (all quotients by 11); no integrality is implied, and the key is not lone in any class.
one_sided_check: Key smallest. Three different error kinds. Not stem-readable: the most natural slip, extrapolating linearly from (0, 0) and (3, 40), gives 4.43 - BELOW the key - and the inverted-ratio k lands above only because 40 > 70/2 here; with W(3) = 25 the same slip lands below.
interior_parity_check: Interior options by value: 14.32 and 21.45 - both two-decimal with nonzero final digit; equally clean.
cheap_bound_check: Cheapest bound: t > 3 (below the key; kills nothing). Every upper estimate needs k first; with k in hand, solving is one linear step, so no check is cheaper than the work. Nearest distractor 14.32 is 18.6% above the key and comes from a slip in that last step.

self_audit.note: Smallest key; t > 3 is the only cheap bound and lies below; no live learning-curve or fitted rational-model row.

topic_tag: piecewise linear function from a table
subskill: distance as area under a piecewise linear speed function
prompt: A cyclist's speed v, in meters per second, t seconds after starting is given at four times in the table below. Between consecutive times listed, the speed changes at a constant rate (so v is a linear function of t on each interval). t (seconds) | 0 | 4 | 10 | 15 ; v (meters per second) | 0 | 12 | 12 | 3. To the nearest tenth of a meter, how far does the cyclist travel from t = 2 to t = 13 ?
explanation: On each piece the distance is the average of the endpoint speeds times the time. v(2) = 6 (halfway from 0 to 12), and on [10, 15] the speed drops 1.8 m/s each second, so v(13) = 12 − 1.8(3) = 6.6. Distance = (6 + 12)/2·2 + 12·6 + (12 + 6.6)/2·3 = 18 + 72 + 27.9 = 117.9 m. The option "120.6" interpolates v(13) from the wrong end, 12 − 1.8(2) = 8.4. The option "112.5" uses the table value 3 at t = 15 as the speed at t = 13. The option "106.5" averages the table speeds over each whole interval and takes the fraction of the interval inside [2, 13]: 24(2/4) + 72 + 37.5(3/5).
quantity_asked: the distance from t = 2 to t = 13 under the piecewise linear speed graph, 18 + 72 + 27.9 = 117.9 m.

distractor_kind.120.6: inverted interpolation fraction for v(13). (a) no parameter extreme. (b) neighbouring setup: none. (c) cheapest bounds: distance ≤ 12 × 11 = 132 (top speed) and ≥ 72 (the [4, 10] stretch alone); 120.6 strictly inside. (d) real: measures 3 s from t = 15 instead of t = 10.
distractor_kind.112.5: next table value used instead of interpolating. (a) no. (b) none. (c) inside (72, 132). (d) real: reads v(13) as 3.
distractor_kind.106.5: whole-interval average speeds prorated by time. (a) no. (b) none. (c) inside (72, 132). (d) real: ignores where in each interval the partial stretch lies.

mechanism: piecewise linear function from a table
distance as area under speed graph
arith_class_check: One-decimal distances; nothing implies integrality, and the key is not lone in any class (two options end in .5, two do not).
interior_parity_check: Interior options by value: 112.5 and 117.9 - both one-decimal three-digit numbers with nonzero tenths; equally clean.

self_audit.note: Interior key; all inside the 72-132 band; no live speed-table accumulation row.

subskill: height of a point on a rotating wheel as a sine function
prompt: A wheel with a radius of 0.8 meter turns counterclockwise at a constant 4 revolutions per second about an axle that is 2.0 meters above the floor. A reflector on the rim is level with the axle and to its right at time t = 0. To the nearest hundredth of a meter, how high above the floor is the reflector at t = 0.29 second?
explanation: The reflector turns through 2π(4) = 8π radians per second, and it starts at the 3 o'clock position moving up, so its height is h(t) = 2.0 + 0.8 sin(8πt). At t = 0.29, 8π(0.29) ≈ 7.288 radians, which is 1.16 revolutions, or 57.6° past the starting position. h ≈ 2.0 + 0.8 sin(57.6°) ≈ 2.0 + 0.675 ≈ 2.68. The option "2.43" uses cosine, as if the reflector started at the top. The option "2.73" treats 4 as radians per second, sin(4·0.29). The option "2.35" treats 4 as seconds per revolution, sin(2π·0.29/4).

distractor_kind.2.43: cosine instead of sine (starting position read as the top). (a) no parameter extreme. (b) neighbouring setup: none. (c) cheapest bounds: 1.2 ≤ h ≤ 2.8; one step finer, 0.16 revolution past 3 o'clock is in the first quarter, so 2.0 < h < 2.8; 2.43 strictly inside. (d) real: start-position slip.
distractor_kind.2.73: revolutions per second read as radians per second. (a) no. (b) none. (c) inside (2.0, 2.8). (d) real: unit slip.
distractor_kind.2.35: rate read as a period. (a) no. (b) none. (c) inside (2.0, 2.8). (d) real: inverts the frequency.

mechanism: height as sine of angle turned
arith_class_check: Two-decimal heights; no integrality implied; the key is not lone in any class.
interior_parity_check: Interior options by value: 2.43 and 2.68 - both two-decimal with nonzero final digit; equally clean.

self_audit.note: Interior key; all options in the first-quarter band (2.0, 2.8). Held AM24F-04 asks time above a level, not a height at a time.

topic_tag: logarithmic model (sound level) with an inverse-square law
subskill: decibel levels at a new distance, then combine intensities
prompt: The sound level L, in decibels, of a sound with intensity I is L = 10 log(I/I₀), where I₀ is a fixed reference intensity. The intensity of the sound from a machine is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the machine, and the intensities of two machines running at the same time add. Machine A produces 82 decibels at a distance of 2 meters, and machine B produces 85 decibels at a distance of 3 meters. A worker stands 6 meters from machine A and 4 meters from machine B. To the nearest hundredth of a decibel, what sound level does the worker hear when both machines run?
explanation: Tripling the distance from A divides its intensity by 9, so A's level is 82 − 10 log 9 ≈ 72.46 dB; going from 3 m to 4 m from B divides its intensity by 16/9, so B's level is 85 − 10 log(16/9) ≈ 82.50 dB. Adding intensities: L = 10 log(10^7.246 + 10^8.250) ≈ 82.50 + 10 log(1 + 10^(−1.004)) ≈ 82.91. The option "83.33" rounds the two levels to 72 and 83 decibels before combining. The option "84.62" treats intensity as inversely proportional to the distance (not its square). The option "85.13" scales by the differences in distance (6 − 2 and 4 − 3) instead of the ratios.
quantity_asked: the combined level at the worker, 10 log(10^((82 − 20 log 3)/10) + 10^((85 − 20 log(4/3))/10)) ≈ 82.91 dB.

distractor_kind.83.33: intermediate rounding of the two levels. (a) no parameter extreme. (b) neighbouring setup: none. (c) cheapest stem-direct bound: each machine is farther from the worker than its reference distance, so the total is below 10 log(10^8.2 + 10^8.5) ≈ 86.76; the total also exceeds the louder single level, which needs B's inverse-square step (the work); 83.33 strictly inside. (d) real: premature rounding.
distractor_kind.84.62: inverse (not inverse-square) distance law. (a) no. (b) none. (c) inside (−, 86.76). (d) real: forgets the square.
distractor_kind.85.13: distance differences instead of ratios. (a) no. (b) none. (c) inside. (d) real: subtracts distances in the scaling factor.

arith_class_check: Two-decimal levels; nothing implies integrality; the key is not lone in any class.
one_sided_check: Key smallest. Three different error kinds (rounding, inverse law, differences). Not stem-readable: swapping the distances (an equally natural slip) gives 80.74, below the key, and rounding moves the result up or down depending on the fractional parts.
interior_parity_check: Interior options by value: 83.33 and 84.62 - both two-decimal with nonzero final digit; equally clean.
cheap_bound_check: Cheapest stem-direct bound: total < 86.76 (each machine quieter at the worker than at its reference distance) - above every option. The lower bound "total > B alone" needs B's level at 4 m, which is half the work, and lies below the key (82.50). Nearest distractor 83.33 is 0.42 dB above the key (a rounding-stage error).

self_audit.note: Smallest key; nearest distractor a rounding-stage slip; no live decibel row (only a Doppler-frequency row, act 7c5578f6).
